subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Wild Coffee Forests
description: A fast breakdown of Wild Coffee Forests for builders.

hook.text: Ethiopia's Kaffa region still has wild coffee forests where the plant grows without any human help.

buildup.text: These forests contain enormous genetic diversity—thousands of wild varieties, most never cataloged.

discovery.text: Wild coffee grows in the shade of taller trees. It needs no irrigation, no fertilizer, no farmers.

twist.text: Deforestation threatens these forests. If they disappear, we lose the genetic key to coffee's future.

climax.text: Scientists race to catalog wild varieties that might resist climate change and emerging diseases.

punchline.text: Coffee's birthplace holds the genes that could save it.

quiz.question: Why are Ethiopia's wild coffee forests important?
options: They contain genetic diversity vital for coffee's future

details.summary: Ethiopia's highland forests are the only place where coffee grows wild. These ancient forests contain immense genetic diversity, with thousands of wild varieties that have never been cultivated. They are a priceless reservoir for developing disease-resistant and climate-adapted coffee strains.
details.whyItMatters: Wild coffee forests hold the genetic key to coffee's future. Losing them to deforestation could leave the entire industry vulnerable to climate catastrophe.
takeaways: Ethiopia's forests are the only place coffee grows wild
They contain thousands of genetically diverse wild varieties
Deforestation threatens this irreplaceable genetic reservoir

faq.question: Why is wild coffee genetic diversity so important?
faq.answer: Cultivated coffee has very narrow genetics, mostly descended from a few plants. Wild varieties may carry genes for disease resistance, drought tolerance, and heat adaptation that breeders desperately need. Losing wild forests eliminates options we may need to save coffee from climate change.

faq.question: How much of Ethiopia's wild coffee forest remains?
faq.answer: Estimates suggest over half has been lost since the 1970s to agricultural expansion and logging. Conservation efforts are underway, including UNESCO biosphere reserves and community forest management programs, but the pace of loss remains alarming.
